tasks.question: How is the scan line stepped across a linear array between successive pulse-echo acquisitions?
tasks.reference_answer: By deactivating an element at one end of the active subaperture and activating a new element at the opposite end.
tasks.rationale: The procedure is explicitly described in the first source paragraph; no visual interpretation is needed.

tasks.question: In Fig. 13.1(c), what geometric feature distinguishes the phased array’s field of view from that of the linear array shown in (a)?
tasks.reference_answer: The phased array produces a converging circular sector FOV that narrows at shallow depths, whereas the linear array yields a rectangular FOV with constant lateral width.
tasks.rationale: The distinction requires comparing the beam contours and shaded regions in parts (a) and (c) of the figure; the text supports but does not fully specify the shape differences without visual confirmation.

tasks.question: Based on the provided page image, what does the dark grey shading in Fig. 13.1(a) represent?
tasks.reference_answer: The active subaperture during acquisition of the indicated scan line.
tasks.rationale: The caption directly beneath the figure in the screenshot states this; the answer depends on reading the figure’s caption in the image, not just the surrounding text.

tasks.question: Correct the following premise: 'A curvilinear array produces a rectangular field of view like a linear array.'
tasks.reference_answer: A curvilinear array produces a circular sector image with a wide field of view at all depths, not a rectangular field of view.
tasks.rationale: The premise is explicitly contradicted by the text stating the curvilinear array yields a 'circular sector image', making correction directly supported by the source.
